config.title: Palindrome Partitioning

intro.title: Palindrome Partitioning
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that solves the palindrome partitioning lesson, which involves splitting a given string into substrings where each substring is a palindrome (reads the same forward and backward). You will learn the core concept of backtracking, a recursive algorithmic technique that explores all possible partitions and discards invalid ones. The main technologies involved are JavaScript functions, recursion, and array manipulation for storing and returning valid partitions. By the end, you will understand how to implement an efficient solution to generate all possible palindrome partitions for any input string.
intro.usecase: Palindrome Partitioning is used in text processing applications like document editors and search engines, where identifying and grouping palindromic segments helps in tasks such as text analysis, plagiarism detection, and optimizing data compression. For example, in a content management dashboard, this algorithm can analyze user-generated text to detect symmetrical patterns for moderation or formatting purposes. Developers implement it to efficiently break down strings into valid palindromic substrings, which is crucial in bioinformatics for DNA sequence analysis and in natural language processing for palindrome-based feature extraction in machine learning models.

objectives: Implement a helper function to check if a substring is a palindrome
Construct a recursive backtracking function to explore partition possibilities
Initialize and update a results array to store valid palindrome partitions
Manipulate string indices to generate substrings for palindrome validation
Integrate the palindrome checker with the backtracking algorithm
Apply the algorithm to partition sample strings into palindrome substrings
Configure the base case for the recursive function to terminate properly

content.body: Welcome! Today we'll explore a fascinating string lesson: finding all the ways to split a string into palindromes. This is like discovering all the beautiful symmetrical patterns hidden within a word. We'll learn a clever approach using backtracking and memoization.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
By the end of this lesson, you'll be able to:
1. Explain what palindrome partitioning means.
2. Apply backtracking to explore different ways to split a string.
3. Use memoization to remember previously computed partitions and avoid redundant work.
4. Implement the complete solution in JavaScript.
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Let's start with a small example. The string "aab" can be split into palindromes in different ways. A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards. What's one way you could split "aab" so each piece is a palindrome?
content.title: Try it
content.prompt: Find one valid palindrome partition for "aab"
content.successMessage: Great thinking! One valid partition is ["a", "a", "b"] since each single character is a palindrome.

content.body: There's another valid partition for "aab". Can you find it? Remember, "aa" is also a palindrome.
content.title: Find another
content.successMessage: Excellent! ["aa", "b"] is another valid partition since "aa" is a palindrome and "b" is a palindrome.

content.body: Now try with "aaba". This has more possibilities. Can you find one valid partition?
content.title: One more challenge
content.successMessage: Well done! One option is ["a", "aba"] since "a" and "aba" are both palindromes.

content.body: What you just did was explore possibilities manually - you tried different splits and checked if each piece was a palindrome. This is the essence of brute force exploration.
content.title: What you did

content.body: For longer strings, manually checking every possible split becomes overwhelming. A string of length n has 2^(n-1) possible partitions! We need a systematic method that's efficient. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: The core idea is to use backtracking to explore partitions, but with a twist: we'll remember what we have already seen. When we find that a substring is a palindrome, we can store this result so we don't check it again later. This is called memoization.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Think of it like a notebook where we write down which substrings are palindromes. Before checking if a substring is a palindrome, we first look in our notebook. If we've already checked it, we just read the answer instead of checking again.

content.body: We'll use backtracking with memoization. Start from the beginning of the string, try different partition points, and only proceed if the current substring is a palindrome. We'll use a memo object to remember palindrome checks.
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
For "aab":
1. Check "a" (palindrome) → explore rest "ab"
2. Check "aa" (palindrome) → explore rest "b"
3. Store results in memo: {"a": true, "aa": true, "ab": false}
4. Build partitions: ["a","a","b"] and ["aa","b"]

content.body:
1. Create a helper function that takes a starting index and current partition.
2. If we reach the end of the string, add the current partition to results.
3. For each possible end position:
   - Get the substring from start to end
   - Check if it's a palindrome (use memo if available)
   - If palindrome, add to current partition and recurse with next start position
   - Backtrack by removing last added substring
4. Use memoization to store palindrome checks for substrings.

content.body:
Congratulations! You've implemented palindrome partitioning using backtracking with memoization. Key takeaways:
1. Backtracking lets us explore all possible partitions systematically.
2. Memoization helps avoid redundant palindrome checks, making our solution efficient.
3. The 'notebook' metaphor (memo object) is a powerful pattern for remembering computed results.
4. Always consider: What do we store as key vs value? (Here, substring indices as key, boolean as value). When do we check the structure vs add to it? (Check before computing, add after computing).
content.title: Done
